The engine currently handles these constraints inconsistently: sometimes it enforces them at the top of the results and then quietly drops them further down; sometimes it ignores them entirely. The most serious cases involve negation, where customers explicitly say what they do *not* want and receive exactly that anyway.

**"Tasche nicht Leder"**
Every single one of the 15 results was a leather bag — Volker Lang Accessoires Handtasche Hirschleder, PB 0110 Rindleder Handybag, Croots Leder-Washbag, Harold's Lederwaren Damen-Backpack Rindleder, and so on through all 15 positions. The word "nicht" (not) was completely ignored. The store does carry non-leather bags, so this is not a catalogue gap — the engine simply has no mechanism to exclude a material when a customer asks it to.

**"Kinderkleidung nicht synthetisch"**
The search returned nothing at all. A customer asking for children's clothing in natural materials — a perfectly reasonable request — was shown a blank page. The engine appears to have tried to find product titles containing the word "synthetisch" and, finding none, returned zero results rather than showing children's clothing with synthetic materials filtered out.

**"Wein ohne Alkohol"**
The two products that directly answer this query — Motzenbäcker Menger-Krug Bio-Riesling alkoholfrei 0,0% and Motzenbäcker Menger-Krug Hakuna Matata Alkoholfreier Schaumwein — were buried at positions 14 and 12. The customer's first eleven results were all standard alcoholic wines, including Weingut Albert Gälweiler Arvalus Rotwein-Cuvée trocken and Weingut Winter Kalkstein Riesling 2024. The word "ohne" (without) was treated as additional context rather than as a hard filter.

**"Gartenleuchte nicht solar"**
Only one product was returned in total — IP44.DE Bodenleuchte Piek Mini — when the full range of non-solar garden lights should have been available. The engine appears to have treated "solar" as a required keyword rather than an excluded one, collapsing the result set to near-nothing instead of returning the full garden lighting assortment minus solar-powered models.

The colour constraint was partially respected at the top but then abandoned. ## Typo Tolerance

Customers make small spelling mistakes constantly — a swapped letter, a missing character, a transposed pair. A well-functioning search engine corrects these silently and returns the right products anyway. At Manufactum, a single missing or transposed character in any query currently produces a completely blank results page, with no correction attempt and no fallback.

**"Tischleuche Sonnenglas"**
One letter dropped from "Tischleuchte" — the 't' — and the search returned nothing at all. The correctly spelled query "Tischleuchte Sonnenglas®" returns the exact product at the top of the results, so the product is well-indexed and highly relevant. A single missing character in a long compound word was enough to produce a complete failure.

**"Umhängetacshe Sonnenleder"**
Two adjacent letters transposed in "Umhängetasche" — 's' and 'c' swapped — and again the search returned nothing. This is one of the most common keyboard error patterns, and the product exists in the catalogue. The engine made no attempt to approximate the query.

**"Kopfbandlupe Binokulra"**
The letters 'a' and 'r' were transposed in "Binokular," producing "Binokulra." The Binokulare Kopfbandlupe is a real product in the catalogue, but the engine returned a blank page rather than recognising the near-match. A customer who knows exactly what they want but makes a single slip on a technical term is left with nothing.

## Prioritized Roadmap

1. **Treat negation words as hard filters, not keywords**
"Nicht," "ohne," and "kein/keine" are being ignored entirely, causing customers who ask for non-leather bags to receive only leather bags, customers searching for alcohol-free wine to see eleven alcoholic wines first, and customers asking for non-solar garden lights to receive a near-empty page — this fixes the Filters & Constraints negation failures across all four affected queries.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Medium Effort

2. **Strip conversational framing and map intent words to product categories**
Queries like "etwas schönes für den Garten verschenken," "Geschenk zum Geburtstag für Gartenliebhaber," "Mitbringsel für Kinder zum Geburtstag," and "ich suche eine schöne Lampe für das Wohnzimmer" all return blank pages because the engine reads them as literal title-match strings — building a layer that extracts the core noun or category intent ("Garten," "Kinder," "Lampe") and discards gift/occasion framing will fix the Language Understanding and Shopping Context zero-result failures simultaneously.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Medium Effort

3. **Add synonym rules for regional, colloquial, and descriptive product terms**
"Rotburgunder" returns nothing while Spätburgunder wines are in the catalogue; "Lupe Stirnband" returns nothing while the Binokulare Kopfbandlupe exists; "Schultertasche" fails to surface Harold's Lederwaren Damen-Schultertasche products because "Umhängetasche" is used in some titles — adding bidirectional synonym mappings for these term pairs (and auditing the catalogue for similar gaps) fixes the Language Understanding synonym failures directly.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Quick Win

4. **Enable approximate matching so single-character errors don't produce blank pages**
A missing 't' in "Tischleuche," a transposed pair in "Umhängetacshe," and a transposed pair in "Binokulra" each produce zero results despite the correct products being well-indexed — configuring the search engine to tolerate one- or two-character differences in longer words will recover these customers automatically without any catalogue changes.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Quick Win

5. **Enforce colour and material constraints as hard filters throughout the full result set**
Colour and material terms in queries — "schwarz," "braun," "Kupfer," "Glas" — are currently treated as soft signals that influence scoring at the top of the page but are dropped further down, allowing the Flos Tischleuchte Lampadina in Orange to appear for a "schwarz" query, non-copper pots to outrank copper ones mid-list, and canvas bags to appear in results for "Umhängetasche aus Leder" — extracting these terms as structured filters applied across the entire result set fixes the Filters & Constraints constraint-dropped failures.
Impact: Moderate | Effort: Medium Effort

6. **Boost the product type noun so it outweighs modifiers and secondary signals in ranking**
Across multiple queries, the engine scores the best match highest but then ranks it below weaker results — for "Tischleuchten," three Filotto Regalleuchte Mensola Magnetica variants (shelf lamps, not table lamps) occupied positions 1–3 while the Audo Copenhagen Tischleuchte Concrete sat at position 11; for "Schreibwaren," two slate boards ranked above the F. Hammann Schreibetui Rindleder despite lower scores — ensuring the product-type head noun carries more weight than brand affinity, recency, or popularity signals will fix these ordering failures across Language Understanding, Product Discovery, and Filters & Constraints.
Impact: Moderate | Effort: Medium Effort

7. **Collapse product variants into a single result card per model**
For "Reisegepäck," the KAZETO spol Schwarzer Pappkoffer mit Holzleisten occupied four of the first five result slots as separate cards, pushing the Croots Reisetasche and Il Bisonte Reisefalttasche Leinen out of view — grouping colour and size variants under one card per model will immediately improve the visible range of products for any search that returns a catalogue with multiple variants.
Impact: Minor | Effort: Medium Effort

### Why This Matters

- **70% of ecommerce sites cannot handle typos** in their site search (Baymard Institute). Sites that do handle them gain a significant edge.
- **~30% of ecommerce visitors use site search**, but they generate a disproportionate share of revenue — search users convert at **1.8–3x the rate** of browse-only visitors (Econsultancy, Algolia).
- **31% of site searches end at a dead end** — irrelevant results or zero results — across the average ecommerce site (Baymard Institute).
- The top 3 results capture **~55–60% of all clicks**. Results below position 3 are seen by a rapidly shrinking share of customers.

## Methodology: The Audit Pipeline

This audit was conducted using our search-quality audit pipeline — a seven-phase automated search quality assessment. 60 test queries were generated across 16 query categories, grouped into 6 core capabilities.

**1. Site Discovery**
Automated analysis of your site's structure, navigation categories, brands, and featured products to understand what your search engine should be able to find.

**2. Test Design**
Site-type-aware selection from a library of 26 test categories. Categories are chosen based on your site's commerce model to ensure the audit tests what matters most for your customers.

**3. Query Generation**
AI-generated realistic customer queries grounded in the actual products, brands, and categories found on your site — not generic templates.

**4. Result Collection**
Automated search execution collecting the top results for each test query exactly as your customers would see them.

**5. Relevance Scoring**
Each result scored on a 0.0–1.0 scale by a specialized relevance model, producing an objective measure of how well each result matches the query intent.

**6. Failure Analysis**
Each query classified by failure mode (e.g., no results, category not understood, constraint ignored, typo not handled, or relevant results buried) and assigned a severity based on customer impact — whether the search returned nothing, surfaced the wrong products, or simply ordered the right ones poorly.

**7. Report Assembly**
Findings synthesized into this actionable narrative with prioritized recommendations ordered by business impact.
